deep.reconstruction:
This page holds anatomical measurements and sketches, not a mathematical derivation. It fits Riemann's late work on the mechanics of the ear ('Mechanik des Ohres', published posthumously in 1867), which is what the bundle name 'R.Ohr' indicates.

(1) Top-left sketch. It almost certainly shows the stapes (stirrup bone) seen from the side. On the left is the head with its articular facet, marked 'l'. The two crura form an arch. On the right is the footplate, drawn as an elongated oval, with an axis line running through it and its ends labelled a and b. The letters v and h above and below probably mean vorn/hinten (anterior/posterior), or perhaps orientation marks such as oben/unten.

(2) Measurement table, headed 'Längste Achse' (longest axis) and 'a'. In the first column, footplate long-axis lengths are recorded: 3 mm for one specimen and 2.75 mm for another. The dashes appear to mean 'same as above' or 'not measured'. In the second column, headed 'a', are values 1.7, 1.5, 1.5, 1.4, 1.2 (marked with '!'), 1.9 in mm. These are presumably the transverse width of the footplate, or a dimension at end a, across several specimens. The '!' flags 1.2 as unusually small.

These figures agree well with modern stapes footplate data: about 3 mm long and 1.2–1.7 mm wide.

(3) 'Gelenkfl.' (Gelenkfläche, articular surface): longest axis 0.75 mm, smallest 0.65 mm. This is most plausibly the incudostapedial facet on the stapes head.

(4) Bottom sketch: a profile of the footplate, or of its rim, set against a vertical line representing the plane of the oval window. A depth or thickness of 0.3 mm is marked. This could be the footplate's curvature or bulge, or its thickness, relative to the window plane.

Purpose (my inference): to quantify the geometry of the stapes and footplate. The aim would be estimating effective areas and lever and hinge relations for Riemann's analysis of how sound is transmitted to the labyrinth. Riemann gives no computation on the page. If one estimates the footplate area as an ellipse (my addition), the result is about π/4·3·1.5 ≈ 3.5 mm².
errors: No derivation is present, so there is nothing to check mathematically.
The labels (v, h, l, a, b) and the meaning of column 'a' are not explained on the page, so interpretation is uncertain.
The 1.2 flagged with '!' is just an outlier remark, not an error.

results.what: Empirical measurements of stapes footplate dimensions (long axis about 2.75–3 mm, width about 1.2–1.9 mm) and of the incudostapedial articular facet (0.75 × 0.65 mm)
results.usually_credited_to: 19th-century otologists and anatomists (e.g. Helmholtz 1868, Henle, Politzer)

results.what: Profile sketch of the footplate relative to the oval-window plane, with a 0.3 mm offset or thickness

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine anatomical measurements. Riemann's interest in ear mechanics is well known through the posthumous 'Mechanik des Ohres'. The page holds no mathematics, only raw stapes data, which is a minor archival detail.

checkable.asserts: The mean of the column-a widths is 92/60 ≈ 1.533 mm
An elliptical footplate 3 × 1.5 mm has area ≈ 3.53 mm² (my estimate, not on the page)
An elliptical articular facet 0.75 × 0.65 mm has area ≈ 0.383 mm² (my estimate)

transcription_corrections: 'Größte Breite[?] 0,75' is more likely 'Längste Achse 0,75', parallel to the heading above.
The heading 'Längste Achse' is plausible. In the image the values 3 mm and 2,75 sit in the first column and the dashes appear as separate entries.
The '!' sits after 1,2 and is correctly placed.
